examples: Does meeting people from other groups change attitudes?

explain.say: Have you ever been nervous about someone new, and then they became your friend? Scientists have studied exactly that. Look at the graph. Across the bottom is real contact with a group; up the side is prejudice. Watch the line fall.

explain.say: First, what is prejudice? Pre-judging: deciding what someone is like before you know them. See the first mark, only stories? When all you know about a group comes from rumours or the news, prejudice is highest. Why might stories alone give a wrong picture?

explain.say: Now look at working together. In 1954 the psychologist Gordon Allport suggested that contact helps most when people share a goal, like a team or a class project. See the line dropping? Can you think of a time a shared goal made you closer to someone?

explain.say: See equal footing? Contact works best when people meet as equals, with fair treatment and support from teachers or leaders. A huge 2006 review of over 500 studies found that contact reduced prejudice in most of them. Why do you think being equals matters?

Contact is not magic; forced or unequal contact can make things worse. Challenge: sit with someone new this week.

faq.a: Prejudice means pre-judging: holding a negative feeling or opinion about people because of the group they belong to, before knowing them. It often grows from stereotypes.

faq.q: Why is prejudice strongest when we only hear stories?
faq.a: With no real contact, all we have are rumours, jokes and news, which often show only the worst or the strangest examples. Our minds fill the gaps with fear.
asks: Why do rumours make prejudice worse?

faq.a: It is the idea, set out by Gordon Allport in 1954, that contact between groups reduces prejudice, especially when people work together towards a shared goal.

faq.q: What makes contact between groups work best?
faq.a: Allport listed four conditions: equal status, shared goals, cooperation rather than competition, and support from authorities like teachers or laws.
Yes. Studies find that cross-group friendships are among the strongest ways to reduce prejudice. Even knowing that a friend has a friend from another group can help.

facts: Gordon Allport set out the contact hypothesis in his 1954 book "The Nature of Prejudice".
Pettigrew and Tropp's 2006 meta-analysis of 515 studies found that intergroup contact usually reduces prejudice.

quiz.say: According to Allport, when does contact reduce prejudice most?
quiz.show: Contact reduces prejudice most when people…

options.show: Meet as equals with a shared goal
options.say: Meet as equals with a shared goal

options.show: Only see each other on the news
options.say: Only see each other on the news

quiz.why: Equal status and a shared goal are two of Allport's key conditions.

wrong.0: Competition can increase hostility between groups.
wrong.2: News is not real contact and can keep stereotypes alive.

quiz.say: On the graph, what happens to prejudice as real contact grows?
quiz.why: The line falls: more real contact usually means less prejudice.

wrong.1: Over 500 studies show it usually changes, falling.
